question: Debugging error test. Which macro makes SQ(2+3) expand to a correct square of the whole argument?
explanation: A safe macro wraps every use of the argument and wraps the whole replacement. Only ((x)*(x)) turns 2+3 into ((2+3)*(2+3)), which is 25. Remember: wrap every macro argument, and wrap the whole replacement.
hint_2: x+x doubles the argument instead of squaring it.
hint_3: Each use of the parameter must be in parentheses, and the whole expression must be too.

question: Debugging error test. malloc succeeds, then the code does *p = 9; free(p); printf("%d", *p); What is the error at the printf?
option_a: free cannot release a single int
option_b: There is no error, because free clears the pointer variable as well as the block
option_c: The only error is that 9 cannot be stored in an allocated int
option_d: The printf uses the object after it has been freed
explanation: free ends the program's right to use that block, but it does not wipe the pointer variable. The later read through that pointer is a use after free, and the language does not promise what it prints. Remember: do not read or write an object after free.
hint: free can release one int, and storing 9 was legal before the free.
hint_2: free does not set the pointer variable to null.
hint_3: The printf uses the block after it was freed.

question: Debugging error test. In if (a) if (b) printf("X"); else printf("Y"); when is Y printed?
option_a: When a is false and b is false
option_b: Whenever b is false, including when a is false
option_c: When a is false and b is true
option_d: When a is true and b is false
explanation: An else belongs to the nearest if, not to the outer if. Y is printed only when the outer test is true, so the inner if is reached, and the inner test is false. Remember: a dangling else belongs to the nearest if.
hint: If the outer test is false, the inner if is never reached.
hint_2: The inner test being false is not enough on its own.
hint_3: The outer condition must be true and the inner condition must be false.

question: Debugging error test. On a normal implementation where int and unsigned int have the same width, what is printed? int i = -1; unsigned int u = 1; if (i < u) printf("yes"); else printf("no");
option_c: A compile-time error, because int and unsigned int cannot be compared
option_d: yes, but only because unsigned int cannot represent 1
explanation: Before the comparison, C converts the signed minus 1 into an unsigned value, and that becomes a very large number. A very large number is not less than 1, so the test fails and the program prints no. Remember: a negative signed value becomes huge when it is converted to unsigned.
hint: Do not compare minus 1 and 1 as ordinary maths here.
hint_2: The comparison is legal, and unsigned can hold 1.
hint_3: The converted left side is huge, so the less-than test fails.

question: Debugging error test. void f(int a[10]) contains sizeof(a). What does that sizeof measure?
option_a: Always 10 times the size of int, because the parameter keeps the array length
option_c: The size of a pointer, because the array parameter has been adjusted to a pointer
option_d: It is a compile-time error in ISO C to apply sizeof to a parameter
explanation: In a parameter list, an array declaration is adjusted to a pointer, so sizeof sees the pointer and not ten ints. The [10] does not preserve a 10-int object inside the function. Remember: an array parameter is a pointer, and sizeof cannot recover the caller's array length.
hint: The [10] does not keep a 40-byte object inside the function.
hint_2: sizeof on a parameter is legal.
hint_3: It measures the pointer, not ten ints.

question: Debugging error test. What is printed? int x = 0; if (x != 0 && 5 / x == 1) printf("A"); else printf("B");
option_c: A floating-point exception, because 5 / x is evaluated
option_d: A compile-time error, because && cannot guard a division
explanation: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation: x != 0 is false, so && does not evaluate 5 / x, and the condition is false. The else branch therefore prints B, and the division by zero does not occur. Remember: && and || stop as soon as the result is known.
hint: Read the code the way the computer reads it, not the way a hurried eye skips the punctuation. && evaluates the right operand only when the left operand is true.
hint_2: Check the ideas that do not fit. The left side is false, so the body that prints A does not run. The division is not reached, and the expression is legal.
hint_3: The line to carry into the exam is this: && and || stop as soon as the result is known.

question: Debugging error test. What is printed? int x = 1, y = 2; if (x & y == 2) printf("yes"); else printf("no");
option_c: A compile-time error, because & and == cannot appear in one condition
explanation: The equality test binds tighter than bitwise AND, so the condition is x AND (y equals 2). y equals 2 is true, and 1 AND 1 is true, so yes is printed. Remember: equality binds tighter than a single ampersand.
hint: Reading it as (x AND y) equals 2 uses the wrong binding.
hint_3: Do the equality first, then the bitwise AND.

question: Debugging error test. int *f(void) { int x = 5; return &x; } What is wrong with f?
option_a: A function cannot return a pointer
option_b: x must be static for any return to compile
option_c: f returns the address of a local variable, which becomes invalid when f returns
option_d: Nothing is wrong, because the caller receives a copy of x's storage
explanation: x lives only while the function is running, so the address sent back to the caller is already dead when the function returns. A static local, or storage from malloc, would outlive the call. Remember: do not return the address of a local variable.
hint: The address is valid only while the function's stack frame exists.
hint_2: Returning a pointer is legal, and the code can compile without static.
hint_3: The returned address refers to a local that has gone out of lifetime.
